newsitem.title: USA: Officials widen search for tainted strawberries.
newsitem.headline: Officials widen search for tainted strawberries.

text.p: Health officials on Friday widened their search for strawberries possibly tainted with the hepatitis A virus that were distributed to up to 250 restaurants, wholesalers and stores in southeastern Michigan.
The strawberries, blamed for 179 cases of hepatitis A in Michigan, were initially thought to be distributed only to school districts, but now it is unclear how many people may have eaten them.

"The hunt continues, and the crazy thing about this is that we don't know where it's going to turn next," said Philip Kirkwood, manager of food service sanitation for the Michigan Department of Agriculture. "We never dreamed that they would be in the public's hands, but they are."

Kirkwood said his agency, working with the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and other state and local authorities, hopes to determine when customers who bought the strawberries last served them.

People who ate the berries within the last two weeks will likely be advised to seek the same immune globulin inoculation given to thousands of schoolchildren in Michigan, Georgia and Los Angeles this week.

The globulin shots contain antibodies that can help them resist or fight off the disease, which produces flu-like symptoms and is rarely fatal. About 10 of those afflicted in Michigan have been sent to the hospital, officials said.

The Caramagno Foods Co. notified state officials on Thursday that it had distributed an undetermined number of 6-1/2-pound containers of Andrew & Williamson brand frozen strawberries in southeast Michigan between May 17 and Dec. 31, 1996.

Geralyn Lasher, a spokeswoman from the Michigan Department of Community Health, said only one commercial establishement in the Detroit area thus far was known to still have Andrew & Williamson strawberries stamped with lot numbers identified as contaminated. Any such berries found will be recalled, she said.
But the state agriculture department is concerned about any strawberries with the Andrew & Williamson label.

"What we're trying to get is how many of the 250 places still have them and what was their last serve date," Kirkwood said. "Anything that came from Andrew & Williamson is suspect, no matter what the lot number is."
Officials with Caramagno Foods in Detroit declined to comment Friday and referred calls to federal officials.

The president of San Diego-based Andrew & Williamson, a unit of Epitope Inc., resigned this week after U.S. Department of Agriculture officials said they suspected that the bad strawberries came from Mexico, and not the United States as required under a USDA school lunch program.
Mexico defended its strawberry farmers on Friday, and said an outbreak of hepatitis A virus in the United States was not clearly linked to exports of the fruit from Mexico.
